extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students or researchers interested in media, satire, and The Onion
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and descriptive practices for producing news-parody content in the style of The Onion: headline-driven satirical pieces that mimic straight news tone to create comedy, while managing audience expectations and legal/ethical risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Headline-first composition process
rubrics_metrics.description: The writers come up with the headlines first. Once a headline is signed off on, the writers craft a story that matches the headline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a defining part of The Onion's creative process (explicitly contrasted with real newsrooms). The headline is the seed of the joke and the story is written to deliver on it. Example: the article notes ‘writers come up with the headlines first… Once a headline is signed off on, the writers craft a story that matches the headline.’

rubrics_metrics.name: Matter-of-fact, Associated Press–style tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Part of what makes the parody work is the matter-of-fact manner in which the articles are written, mimicking the style of the Associated Press.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a straight, objective newsroom voice to heighten the contrast between form and absurd content. The page highlights that this AP-like, deadpan tone is central to The Onion’s comedic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the 'Area Man' / local-newspaper trope to create relatability
rubrics_metrics.description: A recurring theme in The Onion’s stories is the 'Area Man' trope, which uses the local newspaper convention to make news relatable to readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage everyday-local framing and archetypal figures (e.g., 'Area Man') to anchor satire in recognizable experience. The entry cites the trope’s prominence and NPR’s coverage calling attention to its use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure the story matches and delivers on the headline
rubrics_metrics.description: After headline approval, writers craft the story to match the headline so the piece coherently delivers the intended comic premise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The narrative must fulfill the promise or incongruity set up by the headline; alignment between headline and copy is central to effectiveness (page notes the explicit process of matching story to headline).

rubrics_metrics.name: Make nonfactual nature clear (but anticipate misinterpretation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories published in The Onion aren’t true; they are made up for comic effect. However, not everyone always realizes that what they are reading is fake.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Labeling and context can help, but creators should expect some readers or outlets to take satire literally. The page gives examples of misreporting (the 2012 Kim Jong-Un/People example) and emphasizes the editorial reminder 'Remember, none of these are true.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience suitability and age guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: The site is not meant for people under the age of 18 and not everyone finds the same things funny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider intended audience maturity when publishing; provide appropriate warnings or restrictions. The Britannica entry explicitly notes age limits and differing sensibilities among readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercise caution with sensitive or traumatic topics
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor about real tragedies and sensitive topics can provoke serious backlash, be misinterpreted, or cause legal/official scrutiny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page references repeated use of a headline after mass shootings ('No Way To Prevent This…' published 21 times) and notes incidents where attempts at humor led to investigations (a 2011 tweet prompting a Capitol Police investigation). Writers should weigh the comedic value against possible harm and misunderstanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use recurring motifs and headline repetition as rhetorical strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Repetition of a headline or motif (e.g., 'No Way To Prevent This,' used after many mass shootings) can serve as sustained social commentary and become part of a publication’s voice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberately repeating a framing or headline can build a running critique or brand identity; Britannica cites NPR noting The Onion’s repeated headline as an example of this tactic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be prepared to defend satirical speech legally and ethically
rubrics_metrics.description: Satirical publishers may need to assert First Amendment protections and engage in legal advocacy to protect parody as a form of rhetoric.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Britannica documents The Onion filing an amicus brief in a case involving parody and civil-rights claims, noting the organization’s willingness to defend satire’s legal status. Producers should be aware of legal risks and defenses around parody, defamation, and user reactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brand extensions and medium-specific risks
rubrics_metrics.description: Expanding a satire brand into other media (e.g., parody TV network, film, print relaunches) can succeed or fail; medium changes affect reception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Britannica notes ONN (Onion News Network) and The Onion Movie as mixed successes, implying creators should adapt tone and format appropriately when crossing media and expect differing critical and audience responses.
